chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE)

questions.question: Livy says Roman envoys went to study the laws of Athens. Which alternatives do some modern scholars suggest? (select all that apply)
options: They consulted priests in Egypt
Rome borrowed nothing from Greek law
They actually studied the laws of Carthage
They copied the laws of the Etruscans
They visited Sparta rather than Athens
They visited only Greek cities in southern Italy
questions.explanation: Some scholars think the envoys went only to Greek cities in southern Italy, or that Rome borrowed nothing at all. Livy's account mentions Athens and other Greek cities.
questions.sourceQuote: Some modern scholars doubt this, suggesting they visited only Greek cities in southern Italy, or borrowed nothing.

questions.question: What do ancient sources say about the number of tribunes of the plebs before 457 BC?
options: There were first ten, later cut to two
There were first four, two per consul
There were first three, one per tribe
There were first two or five; sources differ
There was always exactly one
There were first twelve, one per table
questions.explanation: Ancient sources disagree, giving either two or five original tribunes. The number rose to ten in 457 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Ancient sources say there were first two or five tribunes, rising to ten in 457 BC.

questions.question: Until what year did the Conflict of the Orders last?
options: 449 BC
264 BC
287 BC
312 BC
367 BC
133 BC
questions.explanation: The struggle lasted until 287 BC. It began less than twenty years after the Republic's traditional founding in 509 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: The long struggle that followed, lasting until 287 BC, is known as the Conflict of the Orders.

questions.question: Which were features of the Twelve Tables' rules on debt? (select all that apply)
options: A tribune could free any chained debtor
A debtor had thirty days to pay
Debts were cancelled every seventh year
Chains had to weigh at least 5 kg (fifteen pounds)
A chained debtor got about 330 g (a pound) of bread a day
Interest was capped at one per cent a year
questions.explanation: After thirty days, a creditor could chain a debtor in fetters of at least 5 kg (fifteen pounds) and feed him about 330 g (a pound) of bread a day for sixty days. The rules were harsh but clear.
questions.sourceQuote: A debtor had thirty days to pay; then his creditor could bind him in chains of at least 5 kg (fifteen pounds) and feed him about 330 g (a pound) of bread a day for sixty days.

questions.question: Besides creating a new protective official, what further concession did the Senate make to end the first secession?
options: The laws were published on bronze tablets
Some plebeians were freed from their debts
One consulship was reserved for plebeians
Plebeians could marry into patrician families
Conquered Sabine land was shared out
Debt slavery was abolished for good
questions.explanation: As well as agreeing to the new official, the Senate freed some plebeians from their debts. The intermarriage ban, by contrast, was later written into the Twelve Tables.
questions.sourceQuote: The Senate agreed, and some plebeians were freed from their debts as well.

questions.question: Roughly how long after the debt crisis of 495 BC did Livy write his account of it?
options: About three centuries later
Within a single generation
About two centuries later
About a century later
Nearly five centuries later
Almost eight centuries later
questions.explanation: Livy wrote nearly five centuries after these events. That gap is a major reason modern historians question the traditional story.
questions.sourceQuote: Livy, the Roman historian who wrote the fullest account of these years nearly five centuries later, tells a story that captures the mood.

questions.question: Even after the Lex Publilia, how did patricians try to tame the tribunes?
options: By making tribunes swear loyalty to the consuls
By having tribunes exiled for sacrilege
By bribing plebeian voters at every election
By persuading one tribune to block his colleagues
By forbidding the Plebeian Council to meet
By cutting the number of tribunes to two
questions.explanation: Patricians tried to turn tribunes against each other, getting one to block his colleagues. Still, the plebs now had a voice and used it to demand written law.
questions.sourceQuote: Patricians kept looking for ways to tame the tribunes, such as persuading one tribune to block his colleagues.

questions.question: What surprising point do historians raise about who the plebeians really were?
options: Many were wealthy landowners
Most were freed slaves from Greece
Many were foreigners without citizenship
Most were members of the priesthood
Most were recent Sabine immigrants
Many were patricians who had lost status
questions.explanation: Many plebeians were wealthy landowners, which complicates the picture of poor commoners against rich aristocrats. It is one of several puzzles about the traditional story.
questions.sourceQuote: And it is unclear who the plebs really were: many were wealthy landowners.

questions.question: What did the two negotiating senators achieve after the second secession of 449 BC? (select all that apply)
options: They cancelled all existing debts
They restored the right of appeal
They lifted the ban on intermarriage
They abolished the consulship
As consuls, they made plebeian decisions binding on all
They restored the tribunes
questions.explanation: The senators restored the tribunes and the right of appeal, and as consuls made plebeian decisions binding on all Romans. Until then, plebiscites had bound only plebeians.
questions.sourceQuote: Two senators negotiated, restored the tribunes and the right of appeal, and as consuls passed laws making plebeian decisions binding on all Romans.

questions.question: According to one modern count, how many secessions did the plebeians stage between 494 and 287 BC?
options: Two
Nine
Twelve
Five
Seven
Three
questions.explanation: One modern count gives five secessions in this period. The first, in 494 BC, set the pattern, and it worked.
questions.sourceQuote: One modern count puts the total at five secessions between 494 and 287 BC.
